title: Desert Foxes: Big Ears, Small Bodies
summary: How the fennec fox and other desert foxes use big ears, furry paws, sandy coats, burrows, and night hunting to survive in hot, dry deserts.
poll: A small animal can survive in the desert better than a big one.

versions.title: Small Fox, Big Ears
versions.text:
Look at this fox. It is small. But its ears are big! It is a fennec fox.

It is the smallest fox in the world. It is as light as a bag of sugar. Its ears are as long as your hand.

It lives in a desert. A desert is a dry land. It has lots of hot sand. It gets very little rain.

Big ears help in two ways. They let heat out. That keeps the fox cool. They help it hear, too. It can hear a bug dig in the sand. The bug is its prey. The fox digs fast to get it.

Thick fur grows on each paw. The fur keeps its feet safe on hot sand.

The day is too hot. The fox naps in a hole. The hole is a burrow. At night, it wakes up to hunt. It is nocturnal.

The fox does not drink much. Its food gives it water. It eats bugs, mice, eggs, and fruit.

Saudi Arabia has a desert fox, too. It is the sand fox. It has big ears and fur on its paws.

versions.title: Small Fox, Big Ears
versions.text:
Look at this fox. Its body is small. But its ears are huge! It is called a fennec fox.

The fennec fox is the smallest fox in the world. It weighs about as much as a bag of sugar. Yet its ears can be as long as your hand.

The fennec fox lives in the desert. A desert is a dry land with lots of sand and very little rain. In the day, it is very hot.

Big ears help in two ways. First, they let heat out of the fox. This keeps the fox cool. Next, they help it hear well. The fox can hear a bug dig under the sand. The bug is its prey. The fox digs fast and catches it.

The fox has thick fur on the bottom of each paw. The fur keeps its feet safe from the hot sand.

When the sun is high, the fox naps in a hole. The hole is called a burrow. At night, the fox comes out to hunt. It is nocturnal, which means it is awake at night.

This fox does not need to drink much. It gets most of its water from its food. It eats bugs, mice, eggs, and fruit.

Saudi Arabia has its own desert fox. It is called the sand fox. It also has big ears and fur on its paws.

versions.title: Desert Foxes: Big Ears
versions.text:
Picture a fox small enough to sit in your hands. Now give it big, long ears. That is the fennec fox!

The fennec fox is the smallest fox in the world. It weighs about one kilogram, like a bag of sugar. But its ears can grow to about fifteen centimeters long.

Fennec foxes live in the desert of North Africa. A desert is a very dry place with little rain. The days are hot, but the nights can be cold.

The big ears do two jobs. First, they help the fox stay cool. Heat leaves the body through the thin skin of the ears. Second, they help the fox hear very well. It can hear a bug or a mouse moving under the sand. That animal is its prey. The fox digs quickly to catch it.

The fox also has thick fur under each paw. This fur keeps its feet from the hot sand. It also helps the fox walk without sinking.

During the hot day, the fox rests in a burrow it digs in the sand. It is cooler there. At night, it comes out to hunt. An animal that is active at night is called nocturnal.

The fennec fox can live a long time without drinking. It gets most of its water from its food, such as bugs, mice, eggs, and fruit.

Saudi Arabia has a desert fox of its own, called the sand fox. It also has large ears and furry paws.

versions.title: Desert Foxes: Big Ears, Small Bodies
versions.text:
Imagine a fox so small that it could fit in a shoebox. Now give it ears that seem far too big for its head. That is the fennec fox, one of the most surprising animals in the desert.

The fennec fox is the smallest fox in the world. An adult weighs only about one kilogram. Its ears, however, can grow up to fifteen centimeters long.

Fennec foxes live in the sandy deserts of North Africa. A desert gets very little rain. The days are very hot, but the nights can be cold.

Those huge ears do two important jobs. First, they help the fox stay cool. Heat from its body escapes through the thin skin of the ears. Second, they give the fox amazing hearing. It can hear insects and mice moving under the sand. When it hears its prey, it digs quickly to catch it.

Thick fur covers the bottom of each paw. This fur protects the fox's feet from the burning sand and helps it walk without sinking.

During the hottest part of the day, the fox stays in a burrow it has dug in the sand, where it is cooler. At night, it comes out to hunt. Animals that are active at night are called nocturnal.

A fennec fox can go a long time without drinking. It gets most of its water from the food it eats, such as insects, mice, eggs, and fruit.

Saudi Arabia has its own desert fox, called the sand fox. Like the fennec, it has large ears and furry paws.

versions.title: Desert Foxes: Big Ears, Small Bodies
versions.text:
Imagine a fox small enough to curl up in a shoebox, with ears that look much too big for its head. This is the fennec fox, and every part of its body helps it live in the desert.

The fennec fox is the smallest fox in the world. An adult weighs only about one kilogram. Yet its ears can grow to fifteen centimeters long. It lives in the sandy deserts of North Africa, where rain is rare. The days are scorching, but the nights can be surprisingly cold.

A body feature that helps an animal survive in its home is called an adaptation. The fennec's ears are a great example. They do two jobs. First, they help the fox stay cool, because heat from its blood escapes through the thin skin of the ears. Second, they give the fox amazing hearing. It can detect insects and mice moving under the sand, and then it digs quickly to catch them.

The fox's thick, sand-colored coat is another adaptation. It works as camouflage, helping the fox blend in with the sand, so predators such as eagles and owls have trouble seeing it. The coat also keeps the fox warm on cold nights. Even the bottoms of its paws are covered in fur. This fur protects its feet from the hot sand and helps it walk on soft dunes.

During the hottest hours, the fox rests in a cool burrow under the sand. It comes out at night to hunt. Fennec foxes often live in small family groups. A mother usually has two to five babies, called kits, in the spring.

The fennec fox is an omnivore, which means it eats both animals and plants. It eats insects, mice, lizards, eggs, fruit, and roots. It can go a long time without drinking, because it gets most of the moisture it needs from its food.

Saudi Arabia has its own desert fox, the sand fox. It also has large ears and furry paws.

versions.title: The Fennec Fox: Built for the Desert
versions.text:
Imagine a fox small enough to curl up comfortably inside a shoebox, with ears that appear almost comically oversized for its delicate head. This is the fennec fox, and practically every characteristic of its anatomy is specifically suited to survival in one of the hottest, driest environments on Earth.

The fennec fox is the smallest fox species in the world. An adult typically weighs only about one kilogram, yet its ears can measure fifteen centimeters in length. It inhabits the sandy deserts of North Africa, where precipitation is scarce, daytime temperatures are scorching, and the nights can become surprisingly cold.

The fennec's enormous ears perform two essential jobs. First, they help the animal dissipate heat, because a network of blood vessels lies just beneath the thin skin, so warmth from the blood can escape into the air. Second, they provide remarkably acute hearing, which enables the fox to detect insects and rodents moving beneath the sand before it digs rapidly to capture them.

Scientists have recognized a broader pattern in nature: mammals that live in hot climates tend to have longer ears and limbs than their relatives in cold regions, because a body part with more exposed surface loses heat more easily. The Arctic fox, by contrast, has small, rounded ears that help it conserve heat in the freezing north. Biologists sometimes describe ears, legs, and tails as extremities. These body parts often reveal what kind of climate an animal is adapted to.

The fox's thick, sand-colored coat provides camouflage against predators such as eagles and owls, and it also serves as insulation during chilly desert nights. Even the soles of its paws are covered with dense fur, which protects its feet from the blistering sand and helps it grip loose dunes.

During the hottest hours, the fox shelters in an underground burrow, emerging after sunset to hunt. Fennec foxes often live in small family groups that share a den, and a mother usually gives birth to two to five kits in the spring.

As an omnivore, the fennec fox eats insects, rodents, lizards, eggs, fruit, and roots. It can survive for long periods without drinking, since it obtains most of its moisture from its food.

Saudi Arabia has its own desert species, the sand fox, which similarly possesses large ears and furry paws.

keyWords.definition: a very dry place that gets very little rain

keyWords.definition: a hole or tunnel in the ground that an animal digs to live in
keyWords.example: The rabbit ran into its burrow when it saw the dog.

keyWords.definition: an animal that is hunted and eaten by another animal
keyWords.example: A small lizard is easy prey for a hungry hawk.

keyWords.definition: awake and active at night instead of in the day
keyWords.example: Owls are nocturnal, so they sleep while we are at school.

keyWords.definition: the foot of an animal such as a cat, dog, or fox

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: How to keep a fox as a pet at home
How desert foxes are built to live in the desert
Why foxes are the biggest animals in any desert
How people grow fruit in the desert
questions.why: The whole article explains how the fox's ears, fur, paws, burrow, and night hunting help it live in a hot, dry desert.

wrong.A: The article never talks about keeping foxes as pets.
wrong.C: The article says the fennec fox is the smallest fox, not the biggest animal.
wrong.D: Fruit is only named as one food the fox eats.

questions.stem: What are the TWO ways big ears help the fennec fox?
options: They keep sand out and help it swim.
They scare away birds and help it climb.
They let heat out and help it hear prey.
They hold water and help it sleep.
questions.why: The article says the ears let heat out to keep the fox cool and help it hear bugs and other prey under the sand.

wrong.A: The article does not say the ears keep out sand or help the fox swim.
wrong.B: The ears do not scare birds or help the fox climb.
wrong.D: The fox gets water from its food, not from its ears.

questions.stem: Where does the fox stay during the hot day?
options: In a burrow under the sand
High up in a tall tree
In a cool river near its home
On top of a big rock
questions.why: The article says the fox rests in a hole, called a burrow, when the day is too hot.

wrong.B: The article does not say the fox climbs trees.
wrong.C: Deserts have very little water, and the article does not mention a river.
wrong.D: A rock in the sun would be hot. The fox goes into its burrow.

questions.stem: The fox is nocturnal. What does nocturnal mean?
options: Very small
Good at digging
Able to live without food
Awake and active at night
questions.why: The article says the fox sleeps in the day and comes out at night to hunt, which is what nocturnal means.

wrong.A: The fox is small, but that is not what nocturnal means.
wrong.B: The fox digs, but nocturnal is about being awake at night.
wrong.C: The fox needs food. Nocturnal is about the time it is awake.

questions.stem: Why does the fox have thick fur on the bottom of its paws?
options: To help it run faster than birds
To keep its feet safe from the hot sand
To help it hold its food
To make its tracks easy to see
questions.why: The article says the fur on its paws keeps its feet safe from the hot sand.

wrong.A: The article does not compare the fox's speed with birds.
wrong.C: The article does not say the fur helps the fox hold food.
wrong.D: The article does not talk about the fox's tracks.

questions.stem: Why can the fennec fox live in a place with very little water to drink?
options: It drinks from the sea each day.
It does not need any water at all.
It gets most of its water from its food.
It stores water in its big ears.
questions.why: The article says the fox does not drink much because its food gives it most of the water it needs.

wrong.A: The article does not say the fox drinks from the sea.
wrong.B: All animals need water. The fox gets it from food.
wrong.D: The ears let heat out. They do not store water.

questions.stem: A fox hears a bug moving under the sand at night. What will it most likely do next?

Run back to its burrow to hide
Go to sleep next to it
Wait until the sun comes up

wrong.C: The fox hunts at night. It would not sleep next to its food.
wrong.D: The fox hunts at night, so it would not wait for the hot day.

questions.stem: Why does the author tell about the sand fox at the end?

To explain how to find and dig up a fox's burrow
To tell readers to stay away from foxes
To show that a desert fox lives in Saudi Arabia, too

wrong.D: The article says the fox lives in sandy deserts where rain is rare, not by a river.

questions.stem: How does the author mainly organize the middle of the article?
options: By telling the fox's life story from birth to old age
By comparing foxes in five different countries
By describing one adaptation at a time and how it helps
By listing steps for building a fox burrow
questions.why: The middle paragraphs each describe a feature, such as the ears, the coat, the paws, or the diet, and explain how it helps the fox survive.

wrong.A: The article mentions kits, but it does not follow the fox's whole life.
wrong.B: The article mainly describes one fox and mentions only North Africa and Saudi Arabia.
wrong.D: The article does not give steps for building a burrow.

MID.prompt: Choose the fennec fox adaptation you think is most important. Explain what it does and why it matters for survival in the desert.
checklist: I named one adaptation and explained what it does.
I gave at least two details from the article.
I explained why it is important for life in the desert.

keyWords.definition: to spread out and disappear, or to make something such as heat do this
keyWords.example: The fog began to dissipate as the sun rose higher.
Dogs have an acute sense of smell that helps them find lost things.

keyWords.definition: to keep something from being lost or wasted
keyWords.example: We turn off the lights to conserve electricity.

keyWords.definition: a body part that sticks out from the main body, such as an ear, leg, or tail
keyWords.example: In very cold weather, your fingers and toes are the first extremities to feel numb.

keyWords.definition: material that keeps heat from escaping or entering
keyWords.example: The thick walls give the house good insulation from summer heat.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Its body and habits are closely suited to desert life.
Arctic foxes are better adapted than fennec foxes.
Fennec foxes are in danger because deserts are growing.
Scientists still do not understand why the fennec has large ears.
questions.why: The article explains how the fox's ears, coat, paws, burrowing, night hunting, and diet allow it to survive heat, cold, and dryness.

wrong.B: The Arctic fox is used only for comparison; the article does not rank them.
wrong.C: The article does not discuss threats to fennec foxes.
wrong.D: The article clearly explains two functions of the ears.

questions.stem: In the article, the ears help the fox "dissipate excess heat." What does dissipate mean here?
options: Collect and store
Let escape and spread away
Create more of and increase
Measure and record
questions.why: The article explains that warmth from the blood escapes into the surrounding air, which is what dissipating heat means.

wrong.A: The ears release heat; they do not store it.
wrong.C: The ears help the fox cool down, not heat up.
wrong.D: The ears do not measure temperature.

questions.stem: Why do large ears help release heat, according to the article?
options: They contain more fur than the rest of the body.
They stay in the shade of the cool underground burrow all day.
A network of blood vessels lies just beneath their thin skin.
They move constantly to create wind.
questions.why: The article says blood vessels lie just beneath the thin skin of the ears, so warmth from the blood can escape into the air.

wrong.A: The article does not say the ears have extra fur.
wrong.B: The burrow provides shade, but that is not why ears release heat.
wrong.D: The article does not say the fox moves its ears to make wind.

questions.stem: How does the Arctic fox's ear shape compare with the fennec's, and why?
options: Its ears are larger, because it must hear prey under snow.
Its ears are the same size, because all foxes are related.
Its ears are pointed, because it lives in forests.
Its ears are small and rounded, which helps it conserve heat.
questions.why: The article contrasts the fennec with the Arctic fox, whose small, rounded ears help it hold in body heat in the cold north.

wrong.A: The article says the Arctic fox's ears are small, not large.
wrong.B: The article contrasts the two ear sizes.
wrong.C: The article does not mention forests or pointed Arctic fox ears.

questions.stem: Based on the pattern scientists have noticed, which animal would most likely have the longest ears?
options: A hare living in a hot desert
A hare living near the North Pole
A hare living on a snowy mountain
A hare living in a cold forest
questions.why: The article says mammals in hot climates tend to have longer ears and limbs than their relatives in cold regions, so the desert hare would most likely have the longest ears.

wrong.B: Animals in cold places tend to have smaller extremities to conserve heat.
wrong.C: A snowy mountain is cold, so long ears would lose too much heat.
wrong.D: A cold forest would favor smaller ears, not longer ones.

questions.stem: What can you infer about why the fox hunts after sunset instead of at midday?
options: Its prey can only be found in burrows during the day.
Night hunting lets it avoid the punishing daytime heat.
Eagles and owls only hunt during the day.
Its fur coat turns dark at night.
questions.why: The article says the days are punishing or scorching and the fox shelters in a burrow during the hottest hours, so hunting at night avoids the heat.

wrong.A: The article says the fox detects prey beneath the sand, but not that prey hides only by day.
wrong.C: Owls are known for hunting at night, and the article does not say this.
wrong.D: The article does not say the coat changes color.

questions.stem: In what order does the article present its information?
options: Kits are born, then they learn to hunt, then they leave the den.
The Arctic fox is described first, then the fennec, then the sand fox.
Size and home, then ears, then a wider pattern, then coat and habits.
The fox's diet, then its predators, then its size.
questions.why: The article first introduces the fennec's size and habitat, then its ears, then the wider pattern about extremities, then its coat, paws, burrow, and diet.

wrong.A: The article mentions kits only briefly and does not follow their growth.
wrong.B: The fennec is introduced first; the Arctic fox appears only as a comparison.
wrong.D: The diet comes near the end, not at the start.

questions.stem: Why does the author include the paragraph about mammals in hot and cold climates?
options: To argue that Arctic foxes should be moved to the desert
To show that the fennec's big ears fit a wider pattern in nature
To explain how scientists measure and compare the ears of many foxes
To prove that all foxes have the same body shape
questions.why: The paragraph connects the fennec's ears to a general pattern, showing that its large extremities are typical of animals adapted to hot climates.

wrong.A: The author never suggests moving animals.
wrong.C: The paragraph does not describe how ears are measured.
wrong.D: The paragraph shows that body shape differs with climate.

HIGH.prompt: Explain how the fennec fox's body solves two different desert problems: extreme heat and finding food. Use the pattern about extremities in your answer.
checklist: I explained how the fox handles heat and how it finds food.
I used the pattern about animals in hot and cold climates.
I supported my ideas with precise details from the article.
